terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. The demo imports a messy export, reads thrown values and asks a fake supplier for quotes, and `npm run types` type-checks your files.

tasks.title: Importing bookings you cannot trust
tasks.description:
In `src/import.ts`:

- Export an interface `BookingRecord` with `id: string`, `customer: string` and `priceCents: number`.
- `isBookingRecord(value: unknown)` is a type guard returning `value is BookingRecord`. It is true only for a non-null object whose `id` and `customer` are strings and whose `priceCents` is a number.
- `readBookings(json: string): BookingRecord[]` parses the JSON. When the result is not an array it throws an `Error` whose message contains `array`. Otherwise it returns only the valid rows, in order. Invalid JSON may throw the parser's own error.

`JSON.parse` returns `any`; put its result straight into a variable typed `unknown` and narrow from there, with no casts. The check calls both functions with hidden rows, including `null`, prices written as text and missing members. It also type-checks your file with hidden code: reading `id` after the guard must compile, and misuse (reading a price as text, passing an array to `readBookings`) must be a type error. Code that uses `any` is rejected.
nextSteps: Write `readBookings` with `unknown`, then run `npm run types` and `node src/demo.ts`.
hints: `unknown` accepts every value, like `any`, but lets you do nothing with it until you have narrowed it. That is exactly what untrusted input needs.
After `typeof value === 'object' && value !== null`, TypeScript lets you write `'id' in value`, and after that `value.id` is readable with the type `unknown`.
`Array.isArray` narrows the parsed data to an array, and `filter` with your type guard as the callback returns `BookingRecord[]`.

tasks.title: Errors you did not throw
tasks.description:
In `src/errors.ts`, `PartNotFoundError` is ready. Write two functions that take whatever a `catch` block caught.

- `errorMessage(error: unknown): string` returns the message of an `Error` (subclasses included), the string itself for a thrown string, the message of a non-null object whose `message` is a string, and `'Something went wrong'` for anything else.
- `describeOrderFailure(error: unknown): string` returns `'Part not found: <part>'` for a `PartNotFoundError` and `'Order failed: <errorMessage(error)>'` for anything else.

The check really throws hidden values (Errors, strings, objects, numbers, `null`, `undefined`) and passes what it caught to your functions. It also type-checks your file with hidden code: passing a caught error, a number or `undefined` must compile, and using the result as anything but a string must be a type error. The parameter must be `unknown`; code that uses `any` is rejected.
nextSteps: Annotate both functions with `unknown` parameters and string results.
Handle objects with a string `message`, then the fallback.
Write `describeOrderFailure` with `instanceof`, then run `npm run types`.
hints: In strict mode the variable in `catch (error)` already has the type `unknown`, because JavaScript can throw anything.
`instanceof Error` narrows to `Error` and covers `TypeError` and your own subclasses. `typeof` handles the string case.
For the object case you need three steps: an object, not `null`, has `message`. Then check that `message` is a string before returning it.

tasks.title: Quotes that can fail
tasks.description:
In `src/quotes.ts`:

- Export `type Result<T, E = string>`: either `{ ok: true, value: T }` or `{ ok: false, error: E }`.
- `getQuote(partId: string, fetchPrice: (partId: string) => Promise<number>): Promise<Result<number>>` is async and calls `fetchPrice(partId)`. It resolves to `{ ok: true, value }` for a finite price of 0 or more, `{ ok: false, error: 'Invalid price' }` for a negative or non-finite price, `{ ok: false, error: <message> }` when `fetchPrice` throws or rejects with an `Error`, and `{ ok: false, error: 'Supplier error' }` when it throws or rejects with anything else. `getQuote` itself never rejects, even when `fetchPrice` throws before returning a promise.
- `unwrapOr(result, fallback)` returns the value of a successful result, or `fallback`. It is generic, and the fallback has the same type as the value.

The check calls `getQuote` with hidden suppliers and `unwrapOr` with hidden results. It also type-checks your file with hidden code: narrowing on `ok` and awaiting the quote must compile, and misuse (reading `value` without checking `ok`, using the quote without `await`, a fallback of the wrong type) must be a type error. Code that uses `any` is rejected.
nextSteps: Write the `Result` type as a union told apart by `ok`.
Wrap the call to `fetchPrice` in `try` and `catch`, and check the price.
Write `unwrapOr`, then run `npm run types` and `node src/demo.ts`.
hints: `ok: true` and `ok: false` are literal types, so `Result` is a discriminated union just like `JobStatus` was.
In an async function, `return { ok: true, value: price }` is enough. The `Promise` around it comes from the `async` keyword.
Put `await fetchPrice(partId)` inside the `try`. A sync throw and a rejected promise then both land in the same `catch`, where the caught value is `unknown`.
